common_name: Neves Azorean Red Tomato (Portuguese-American Heirloom Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Neves Azorean Red is a Portuguese-American heirloom brought to the United States by Azorean immigrant families and preserved through home seed saving, valued for its huge, meaty, low-seed fruit.

directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date and provide sturdy staking, since the vigorous indeterminate vines carry a heavy load of large fruit. Neves Azorean Red traces to Azorean immigrant families who brought tomato seed with them to New England and California and kept it going in home gardens for generations before it entered the wider heirloom seed trade; the deep pinkish-red beefsteak fruit is prized for its dense, meaty flesh, relatively small seed cavities, and low acidity, which makes for a tomato with almost no watery waste when sliced. Individual fruits commonly reach a pound or more on well-grown plants, and the rich, well-balanced flavor holds up in sandwiches and fresh salads as well as in sauce. As an open-pollinated heirloom it saves true from seed with basic isolation, letting gardeners keep the family line going the same way it has been passed down for decades.

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring; Willamette is an Oregon State University release that became the backbone of Pacific Northwest commercial red raspberry production for decades and remains a dependable summer-bearing home garden variety.

directions: Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil, and support the upright canes with a simple wire trellis to keep the heavy midseason crop off the ground. Willamette was released by Oregon State University and for much of the twentieth century was the standard red raspberry of the Pacific Northwest processing industry, valued for firm, richly flavored, deep-red berries that hold together well for freezing and canning as well as fresh eating. The floricanes bear a single concentrated crop in early-to-mid summer, and the plant's moderate vigor and reasonable disease tolerance made it a dependable choice for both commercial fields and home gardens for generations. It prefers the cooler summers of its native range and, like most red raspberries, is a more marginal performer in hot, humid climates, so give it the coolest, best-drained spot available outside the Pacific Northwest. Remove spent floricanes after harvest and thin new canes each spring to the sturdiest four or five per foot of row.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in late winter; Osage is part of the USDA pecan breeding program's series of cultivars named for Native American nations, alongside Kanza, Lakota, Choctaw, Sioux, and Oconee, and is grown for reliable production on a moderately vigorous tree.

directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and pair with a compatible pollinator of the opposite pollen type for full production, since pecans do not reliably self-pollinate. Osage belongs to the USDA pecan breeding program's family of cultivars named for Native American nations, developed to give growers better disease resistance and more consistent bearing than many older heirloom pecans, particularly in humid regions where pecan scab is a persistent problem. It produces medium-sized, good-quality nuts with a solid kernel percentage on a tree that begins bearing at a relatively young age for a pecan. As with other pecans, deep, well-drained soil and a large amount of room to grow are essential, since mature trees can eventually reach well over sixty feet with a comparably wide canopy. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer, since drought stress at that stage is the most common cause of poor kernel fill.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service Pecan Breeding Program

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Davis is an American elderberry cultivar grown alongside Adams, York, and Nova as a cross-pollination partner, with a second cultivar nearby giving a substantially heavier crop than a single variety planted alone.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and plant at least one other named elderberry cultivar nearby, since elderberries set a far heavier crop with cross-pollination than they do alone. Davis is a selected American elderberry cultivar grown for its broad, flat clusters of small white flowers in early summer, useful for elderflower cordial and fritters, followed by heavy clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late summer that are cooked into syrup, jelly, and wine rather than eaten raw. Like other American elderberry cultivars it spreads by root suckers to form a multi-stemmed thicket if left unmanaged, so remove unwanted suckers each season to keep the planting to a defined shrub. Elderberry prefers consistently moist soil and performs best in a low spot or near a downspout where it won't dry out during summer heat; prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the shrub vigorous and productive.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring before bud break; Prolific is one of the older named pawpaw cultivars, selected and propagated by grafting for its unusually heavy, consistent bearing rather than for the largest possible fruit size.

directions: Plant in partial shade while young, since pawpaw seedlings and young trees are naturally understory plants that scorch in full sun, and transition the tree to more sun as it matures and begins bearing. Prolific is one of the longer-established named pawpaw cultivars grown for grafted orchards, valued less for exceptional fruit size than for its dependable, heavy annual crops of medium fruit with good flavor, making it a useful workhorse variety in a mixed planting. Like all pawpaws it needs cross-pollination from a genetically distinct cultivar to set a full crop, since a pawpaw's own pollen rarely fertilizes its own flowers well, so plant it alongside a different named variety or seedling tree flowering at the same time. The maroon, unpleasant-smelling flowers are pollinated primarily by flies and beetles rather than bees, and hand pollination with a small brush can improve fruit set in a planting with poor natural pollinator visits.
